transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose I should start from the beginning, or at least what feels like the beginning of all this. What brings me in today is... well, it's this feeling that just won't go away. Ever since my friend was killed, I've been living with this constant, heavy mix of emotions. It's like I wake up and there's this immediate wave of guilt, you know? Wondering what I could have done differently, even though logically I know I wasn't there, but the mind just spins and spins. And then there's the fear, this terrible, clinging fear that something awful is going to happen again, just out of the blue, like it did to her. And underneath it all, or maybe right on top of it, is just so much anger. Anger at the world, anger at the unfairness of it all. People kept telling me, you know, my sister, my neighbors, they all said, "Oh, time heals all wounds," or "It'll get easier as the months go by." But it hasn't. It hasn't eased at all the way everyone seemed to think it would. If anything, it feels like it's settled into my bones, this constant state of just... feeling awful, every single day. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter how much time passes or what I try to do to distract myself. It's just always there, this dark cloud of guilt and fear and anger, just following me around from the moment I wake up until I finally manage to fall asleep.
Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about your friend's death in a way that feels intrusive or uncontrollable?

Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, constantly. It's... it's like I have absolutely no control over my own mind anymore, which is just a terrifying feeling. I'll just be going about my day, trying to run a simple errand, maybe walking down to the pharmacy or the market, and out of nowhere, it just takes over. 

It doesn't even have to be anything significant, either. The most mundane, everyday things will just hijack my brain entirely. For instance, just hearing the deep, heavy growl of a truck shifting gears down the street, or... or the chirping sound of a crosswalk signal changing. Even something as innocent as glancing at one of those walking-tour maps they have set up on the sidewalks downtown. 

The second I encounter one of those things, it's like a switch flips and the whole scene is suddenly put right back into my head. And I mean so sharply, so vividly, that I am right back there. I can see my friend stepping off the curb, right there in my mind's eye, and it happens before I can even try to stop it. I see her foot go down, and my mind is just screaming at her to wait, but the image is already there, playing out in this awful loop. I can't stop the thought, I can't push it away or think about something else. I just stand there, completely frozen, replaying that exact split second. It takes me so long to just catch my breath and realize I'm standing in front of a map in the present day, not back on that street corner. It's just so exhausting, doctor, because I never know when it's going to hit me next. I mean, how do you avoid crosswalks and trucks? You can't. So I'm just constantly at the mercy of these images rushing back in...
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, people, or activities because they remind you of your friend's death?

Well, yes. Yes, I do, and it's become quite a burden, to be perfectly honest. I mean, I go completely out of my way to avoid that intersection now. I will literally drive an extra fifteen or twenty minutes, taking all these winding back roads through the residential neighborhoods, just to make sure I don't even come within a mile of the place. Even if I just need to get to the grocery store or the post office, which used to be a simple five-minute trip straight down the main avenue, I just... I can't do it. I find myself mapping out these ridiculous, convoluted alternate routes in my head before I even grab my car keys. 

And it's not just the physical places, either. It's the activities I used to love. I used to be so active, you know, now that I'm retired. But I have completely stopped signing up for most of the walking tours I used to enjoy so much, and I even had to step down from the neighborhood watch and the safety meetings. I just... I cannot bear the conversations. Whenever a group gets together, especially the safety committee, the talk always, inevitably, circles back to what happened there. Someone will bring up pedestrian right-of-ways, or traffic calming measures, or they'll just casually mention her name and the accident, and I feel like the air is just sucked right out of the room. I can't sit there and listen to them dissect it, or offer their little opinions on city planning while I'm sitting there reliving the worst day of my life. It's just too much. So I just stay home. I cancel my RSVPs, I ignore the sign-up sheets... it's just easier to avoid it all entirely than to risk being ambushed by people talking about it.
Do you often find yourself on the lookout for potential dangers or threats in your daily life?

Oh, constantly. It is absolutely exhausting, to tell you the truth. Whenever I am anywhere near a road—and I mean, you can't really avoid roads entirely, can you? Even if I take those convoluted back routes I was just telling you about, there is always still traffic. And the very moment I am near it, whether I'm walking on a sidewalk or driving my own car, my eyes are just darting everywhere. I can't just relax and exist in the world anymore. 

I watch every single truck that passes by, analyzing how fast it's going, how close it is to the shoulder, whether the driver looks like they might be distracted. I watch the curbs, checking to see if anyone is standing even a fraction of an inch too close to the edge. And the pedestrians... oh, I watch every single pedestrian. It's this overwhelming feeling, doctor, like... like it is my absolute personal responsibility to catch the danger before it happens again. 

It feels like if I just look hard enough, if I just pay enough attention to every little detail around me, I can somehow stop another tragedy from occurring. I'll be clutching my purse so hard my knuckles turn white, just staring at some stranger waiting to cross the street, practically holding my breath until they make it to the other side. I just can't turn it off. I have to monitor everything. Every truck, every curb, every person walking by. It's like I've been appointed the safety officer for the entire world, and if I blink, or if I look away for even a second, someone is going to get killed. I know logically I can't control what happens to other people, but my brain just won't let me let my guard down. I just have to keep scanning, scanning, scanning...
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, I suppose I have. In fact, I know I have. It's... it's quite sad, really, when I sit down and think about it. I used to have such a full schedule, doctor. I mean, my calendar was always just bursting with things to do. I used to spend hours, absolutely hours, planning out my garden beds every spring. I'd sketch out where the hydrangeas would go, and how to rotate the perennials... I took such pride in it. And I had my quilting circle with the ladies on Tuesdays, which was always just a wonderful time to catch up and create something beautiful together. We'd have tea, and sometimes someone would bring a lemon cake... 

And the theater outings! Oh, we used to organize these lovely group trips to the local playhouse, getting dressed up and going out for dinner beforehand. And my book club, too. I used to love our book club meetings. I was always the one who would get into these spirited, happy little arguments about the characters' motivations or the author's pacing. I was so engaged, you know? I felt so alive and connected to my community and my hobbies. 

But now... now I just look at those things written on the calendar, the ones I haven't bothered to erase yet, and I just feel... nothing. It's the strangest sensation. It's like I'm looking at a schedule that belongs to a completely different person. Someone I used to be, a long time ago, before everything changed. The thought of sitting in a circle quilting, or arguing about a novel... it just seems so pointless now. I can't muster up even an ounce of the enthusiasm I used to have. The energy it would take to even pretend to care about those things just feels entirely beyond me. I just sit in my house and look at the garden out the window, and I don't even care that the weeds are starting to take over the flower beds I used to tend so carefully. It's all just... it's just gone. The joy of it is just gone.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things that were once important to you?

Well, yes, doctor, that's exactly what I was just trying to explain... it's exactly that. Those things that were so incredibly important to me, the absolute center of my week—I really can't emphasize enough how much I used to live for them. 

Like I was just saying about the garden beds—I used to spend the entire winter pouring over seed catalogs, mapping out the precise color coordination, making sure the soil was just right. It was a passion. And my time quilting with the ladies, and all those lovely theater outings we'd get so dressed up for, and the book club where I'd just happily argue away about the chapters... those weren't just passing hobbies, they were my life. They were what made me, well, me. 

But now? Now I just look at those things written on the calendar, the dates I haven't crossed out, and I feel... absolutely nothing. It's the most bizarre, hollow feeling in the world. I stare at the reminders on my fridge and it truly feels like those appointments, those passions, they belong to someone I used to be. A completely different woman. It's like reading a stranger's itinerary. The weeds are growing up through the mulch, the books are sitting unread on my nightstand, and I just... I can't find it in myself to care, no matter how much time I spend sitting in my living room thinking about how I really *should* care. I just don't.
Do you feel like you're no longer the person you used to be before your friend's death?

Yes, yes, that's it entirely. I mean, I really feel like I'm just a ghost of the woman I was. It's like I was telling you before, about the garden and the quilting and the book club... I was such a vibrant person, doctor. I really was. I was the kind of person who would wake up early on a Saturday just to get to the farmer's market for the best tomatoes, and then I'd spend the afternoon baking, and the evening at the theater. I was always doing something, always engaged with people, always, well, alive. 

But since... since she died, since that awful day, it's like someone just flipped a switch and turned off all the color in my world. I look in the mirror and I see the same face, the same wrinkles I've earned over the years, the same white hair, but the woman looking back at me just isn't the same person who used to plan those elaborate garden beds or argue so passionately about a novel. I look at my calendar, with all those things I used to love written on it, and it really does feel like I'm reading the schedule of a stranger. I just feel so disconnected from that life, from that joy. It's like the woman who loved those things died on that road, too, and I'm just... I'm just what's left behind.
Do you ever feel like you're outside of your body, watching yourself from afar?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I've heard people talk about things like that, you know, on those television programs or in books where someone has a near-death experience and they float up to the ceiling and look down at the doctors working on them. I always thought that sounded so fantastical, didn't you? But no, I've never felt anything quite like that. 

I feel very... stuck in my body, if that makes sense. Too stuck in it, sometimes. I feel the heaviness of it, the way my joints ache a little more these days, the way I just sit in my chair by the window and feel the weight of gravity holding me down. I'm definitely in here. I'm not floating away or watching myself from the corner of the room. I'm just sitting here, feeling hollow. I suppose sometimes I wish I *could* float away, just to get a break from the constant feeling of... well, of not being who I used to be. But no, doctor, I don't have those out-of-body experiences. I'm very much grounded in this reality, as gray and empty as it feels right now. It's just me, sitting here, looking at the garden and not caring about it.
Are there any activities that you still find yourself looking forward to or enjoying?

Well, I... I really don't think so. I've tried, doctor, I really have. I'll sit there in my armchair, the one with the floral upholstery by the window, and I'll think to myself, "Surely there must be something." But it all just circles back to what I was telling you earlier. It's so frustrating, because I know I *should* look forward to things. 

Like, I used to spend hours, absolute hours, planning my garden beds for the spring. I'd have my graph paper out, my colored pencils, making sure the daffodils would bloom right before the tulips, and that the hostas wouldn't overshadow the impatiens. And quilting with the ladies on Tuesdays—that was a staple! We'd have tea and shortbread and just talk for hours while we worked. And the theater outings... oh, we used to get season tickets and dress up so nicely, maybe get dinner beforehand at that little Italian place downtown. And my book club, where I'd just happily argue away about the characters' motivations until we were all laughing. 

But now... I just look at the calendar hanging on the kitchen wall, the one with the Thomas Kinkade paintings, and I see those things written there. I see "Book Club, 7 PM" or "Quilting at Martha's," and I feel... well, I feel almost absolutely nothing. It's just a blankness. It truly feels like those activities, those joys, they belong to someone I used to be. Like I'm looking at a schedule for a completely different woman who just happened to live in my house. I don't look forward to any of it anymore. I just don't have the energy or the... the spark for it. It's all just gone.
Do you feel like you still enjoy or find pleasure in any activities at all?

Well, doctor, it's just like I was saying a moment ago, isn't it? It's... it's really the same thing. I sit there and I try to find a spark, just a tiny glimmer of the pleasure I used to take in things, but it's just not there. I mean, think about my garden. I used to spend the whole winter, when the ground was frozen solid and there was snow piled up to the windowsills, I would sit at the dining room table with my seed catalogs. I would plan out every square inch of those garden beds. I'd map out where the zinnias would go, and how the climbing roses needed to be trained on the trellis... I took such joy in it. Such immense, profound joy. 

And then there were my Tuesdays with the quilting ladies. Oh, we had such a wonderful time. Martha would always make her famous lemon squares, and we'd sit around the frame, our needles just flying, talking about everything under the sun—our grandchildren, the news, the neighborhood gossip. It was a highlight of my week. And the theater! Getting dressed up, putting on a nice string of pearls and my good wool coat, going out to see a play... and the book club, where we'd debate and laugh until our sides ached... 

But now? Now I look at the calendar hanging there in the kitchen, and I see those things written down—the meetings, the reminders to start the seedlings—and I just... I feel almost absolutely nothing. It's a terrible, heavy kind of nothing. It's exactly as I said before, it feels like those activities, those passions, they belong to someone I used to be. A completely different woman. I look at the words on the page and I don't feel a drop of pleasure or anticipation. It's just blank. So, no, doctor, I don't think I find pleasure in any of it anymore. It's all just... gone.
Are there any small things that still bring you a bit of happiness or comfort?

I know you're asking about the small things now, doctor, maybe hoping there's some little loophole or a tiny exception to what I've been saying, but... well, I feel like a terrible broken record, I really do. It all just circles right back to exactly what we've been talking about for the last ten minutes. 

Even the smallest things, the tiny comforts I used to have... they were all wrapped up in those exact same activities. The small comfort of the garden wasn't just the big blooming flowers, it was the feeling of the graph paper under my hand when I used to plan the beds, or the smell of the potting soil. The small happiness in quilting with the ladies wasn't just finishing a blanket, it was the sound of the thread pulling through the fabric, or the taste of the tea we'd drink. The rustle of the playbills at the theater outings, the cozy feeling of the living room when we'd argue happily at book club... those *were* my small things. Those were my comforts. 

And I know I keep saying this, but I don't know how else to explain it to you—I look at those things on the calendar now, all those little moments that made up my life, and I feel almost absolutely nothing. I wish I could give you a different answer. I wish I could say, "Oh yes, watching a bird at the feeder brings me a bit of joy," but it just doesn't. The woman who loved the garden, who loved getting dressed up for the theater and laughing with her friends... she's the one who felt comfort. But now, it truly feels like all of that belongs to someone I used to be. I just sit here and stare at the dates on the wall and there's no comfort to be found in any of it. I'm sorry to keep repeating myself, but I just can't seem to find a single thing that hasn't been swallowed up by this... this blankness.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure from things that would normally bring you happiness?

Doctor, I... I feel like we are just going in circles, I really do. I don't mean to be difficult, but aren't you just asking me the exact same thing again? Yes. Yes, I am completely unable to experience pleasure from those things. It's exactly what I've been trying to explain for this entire appointment. 

All those things that would normally bring me happiness... I mean, I used to plan my garden beds with such meticulous care, mapping out every little detail for the spring. I used to quilt with the ladies, and we'd have such wonderful afternoons. I used to go to those theater outings all dressed up, and I used to argue happily at my book club until my sides ached. Those *were* the things that normally brought me happiness. That was my life, doctor. 

And now I sit in my kitchen, and I look at those exact things written on my calendar, and I feel almost nothing. It's just a complete void where the joy used to be. It truly feels like all of it—the gardening, the quilting, the theater, the books—like they belong to someone I used to be. A completely different woman who just happens to share my name and live in my house. So, yes, I am unable to experience pleasure from them. I don't know how many different ways I can describe it to you, it's just... the happiness is completely gone.
Do you feel like you're unable to feel happy or excited about anything in your life right now?

Doctor, I... I just don't understand why we keep going over this exact same ground. It's... it's like I'm speaking a different language, or maybe I'm just not explaining myself properly, though I truly feel I've tried. I've laid it all out for you, haven't I? 

When you ask if I can feel happy or excited about *anything*... well, what is there besides the things that made up my life? I told you about how I used to spend hours, absolutely hours, planning out my garden beds. I can still picture the graph paper, the little colored pencils I'd use to mark the different varieties of tomatoes and the marigolds... I used to get so *excited* about that. I would count down the days until the last frost. And the quilting with the ladies—the excitement of seeing a pattern come together, the joy of just being in that room with them, laughing and talking. The theater outings... oh, the anticipation of the house lights going down, the murmur of the crowd... and my book club, the thrill of a really good, spirited debate over a novel we all read... 

Those were the things that made me happy. Those were the things that brought excitement to my life. And I have told you, I think three times now, that when I look at the calendar in my kitchen—the one with the little pictures of birds on it—and I see those exact activities written there in my own handwriting, I feel almost nothing. No happiness. No excitement. Not a flutter in my chest. It's just... flat. It's like I'm reading a schedule for a stranger, like all of those passions and all of that excitement belong to someone I used to be. A ghost of a woman who isn't sitting in this chair right now. So, please, doctor, I don't know what else to say... the answer is no, I don't feel happy or excited about anything anymore, because the things that used to do that for me are just... they're just dead to me now.
Do you feel like your loss of interest in activities is something that has been very noticeable to you and those around you?

Doctor, I... I honestly have to ask, are you listening to me? Or is this some kind of... of memory test? Because I feel like I am trapped in a loop here. I have just spent this entire appointment explaining exactly this to you. Yes, it is noticeable to me. How could it not be? It's the only thing I *can* notice! And of course it's noticeable to those around me. The ladies from my groups, they call and they leave voicemails, asking if I'm coming down with a cold or if I'm out of town, because I've just completely vanished from my own life. 

I don't mean to snap at you, I really don't, but as I have said over and over... I used to plan my garden beds, I used to quilt with the ladies, I used to go to all those theater outings, and I used to argue happily at book club. My friends notice I'm gone because I was always the one organizing the carpool to the theater, or bringing the tea to the quilting circle! And now... now I just sit in my house. I look at those exact things written on the calendar, all those plans I made, and I feel almost nothing. 

I've told you this. It feels like they belong to someone I used to be. The woman who did those things, who cared about those things, is gone, and everyone who knows me can see it just as clearly as I can. Please, doctor, I'm begging you, can we please talk about something else? I really can't bear to explain the garden and the calendar to you one more time.
How long have you been feeling this way since your friend's death?

Well, it's... oh, it's been quite a while now. Let me think. It was... yes, it was two years and three months ago. Two years and three months since that awful day. 

We were on that walking tour, you see. It was supposed to be such a lovely trip. We had planned it for ages, looking at brochures, picking out the right walking shoes, talking about all the historic sites we were going to see. She was so excited about the architecture. And then... well, then it happened. She was killed right there on the tour. It was just so sudden, so horribly sudden, and... and everything just stopped. 

That was when this whole... this heavy, gray cloud just descended on me. Two years and three months of waking up and feeling like I'm just going through the motions of someone else's life. I remember coming home from that trip—coming home alone—and walking into my house, and it was like all the color had just been drained out of the world. The calendar was still hanging there in the kitchen, with all our plans written on it, and I just stood there staring at it, realizing she was never coming back and that I... I didn't care about any of those plans anymore. So, yes, it's been exactly that long. Two years and three months of this absolute emptiness since I lost her.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of guilt related to your friend's death?

Well, it's... it's been the whole time, doctor. The entire two years and three months. And it's not just the guilt, though heavens know that's heavy enough on its own. It's this... this constant, churning mix of things. Guilt, yes, but also fear, and this terrible, deep-seated anger. 

I remember people telling me, right after it happened, right after I came back from that dreadful walking tour... they would bring casseroles and say, "Time heals all wounds," or "It will get easier, you just have to give it a year." They all seemed so certain that the sharp edges of it would dull down. But they haven't. Not one bit. If anything, it's just settled into my bones. 

I wake up with it, this awful dread in my stomach, and I go to sleep with it. I'll be sitting there, trying to drink a cup of tea, and suddenly I'm just so furious that she was taken like that, and then I'm terrified because the world just feels so incredibly unsafe, and then the guilt washes over me again because I was there and I survived and she didn't. Why her and not me? We were standing right next to each other. I just... I can't shake it. It hasn't eased up the way everyone promised me it would. It's just a constant, heavy weight, every single day since she was killed.
